passages.t: Men who came to David before he was king
passages.happening:
‘Now these were the men who came to David at Ziklag, while he was still banished from the presence of Saul son of Kish’ (verse 1). They are archers ‘using both the right and left hands to sling stones and shoot arrows’, and they are Saul's own kinsmen from Benjamin (verse 2). Gadites cross over to David's desert stronghold, men ‘whose faces were like the faces of lions and who were as swift as gazelles on the mountains’ (verse 8), crossing the Jordan in flood (verse 15).

When men of Benjamin and Judah come, David meets them: “If you have come to me in peace to help me, my heart will be united with you” (verse 17), but if to betray him, may God judge. ‘Then the Spirit came upon Amasai, the chief of the Thirty’ (verse 18), and he says, “We are yours, O David! We are with you, O son of Jesse! Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers, for your God helps you” (verse 18). Men from Manasseh come too, and day after day more come to help David, ‘until he had a great army, like the army of God’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 12 steps back in time to show how the kingdom came to David. Even while Saul lived and David was an outlaw, men from Saul's own tribe, from Gad across the Jordan, from Judah and from Manasseh came over to him. None of this chapter appears in Samuel, so the Chronicler drew on sources that are now lost.

Ziklag was the town the Philistine king of Gath gave David while he lived among the Philistines. Benjamin was known for fighters who could use either hand. Crossing the Jordan in the first month, in spring, when the river is swollen with rain and snowmelt, was dangerous, and it showed how determined they were.

An outlaw leader had to decide quickly whether newcomers were friends or spies. David's words are a conditional oath. Amasai's answer is a pledge of loyalty in a short poem. Literally, the Spirit clothed Amasai, the same vivid phrase used of Gideon. The key word of the chapter is help, azar, which comes again and again: men came to help David, and Amasai says David's God helps him. Human help and God's help work together, with God's as the foundation. Peace, shalom, is said three times: more than the absence of conflict, the full flourishing of a relationship set right.
passages.later: The same phrase is used of Gideon in Judges: ‘So the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon’ (Judges 6:34).
passages.asks: Men came to David when he was still an outlaw, before there was anything to gain. Ask whom you would stand with before it was safe to do so. And ask what it would mean for you to say to God what Amasai said to David.

passages.t: All the tribes at Hebron, and three days of joy
passages.happening:
‘Now these are the numbers of men armed for battle who came to David at Hebron to turn Saul’s kingdom over to him, in accordance with the word of the LORD’ (verse 23). Tribe by tribe they are counted (verses 24-37). From Issachar come ‘men who understood the times and knew what Israel should do’ (verse 32).

‘All these men of war, arrayed for battle, came to Hebron fully determined to make David king over all Israel. And all the rest of the Israelites were of one mind to make David king’ (verse 38). They spend three days eating and drinking with David, and neighbors from as far as Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali bring food on donkeys, camels, mules and oxen. ‘Indeed, there was joy in Israel’ (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
This is the assembly at Hebron, where David was made king over all Israel around 1003 BC, after seven and a half years as king of Judah. The tribes are listed roughly from south to north, ending with the tribes east of the Jordan. The chapter moves from a trickle to a flood, and it ends not with a battle but with a feast.

The coronation feast was a covenant meal as well as a celebration: eating together sealed the bond between king and people, and provisions from the far north show the whole land taking part. The men of Issachar who understood the times have become a byword for wise discernment, reading a situation in the light of God's purposes.

For the Chronicler this is Israel as it should be: all the tribes united under the king God chose, with joy. It sets the stage for bringing the ark to Jerusalem.
passages.later: Jesus spoke of a feast to come: ‘many will come from the east and the west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 8:11).
passages.hard:
Are the troop numbers meant literally, and why is Judah's so small?

Verses 24 to 37 total roughly 340,000 men, and the distribution is surprising: Judah, David's own tribe, sends 6,800, while Zebulun sends 50,000 and the eastern tribes 120,000. Readers handle this in different ways. Some take the numbers at face value, noting that it was a national gathering and the far tribes had to show their support in strength. Others argue that the Hebrew eleph, usually translated thousand, sometimes means a military unit or clan, so that a figure like 6,800 might first have meant six units totaling eight hundred men; on that reading the totals become much smaller. Others see the numbers as expressing the Chronicler's point that the whole nation, the distant tribes included, overwhelmingly supported David. Each view has scholarly defenders. On any reading the chapter says plainly that all Israel, not just Judah, was of one mind to make David king.
passages.asks: The men of Issachar understood the times and knew what Israel should do. Ask what your own times are asking of God's people, and whether you understand them. And ask when your church last ended a hard season with a feast.
